item.title: A Rural Village Voted to Leave the U.K., Stirring Britain’s Migration Debate
item.description:
“What a week we’ve had,” a triumphant Tim McNally told dozens of his neighbors in Piddington’s village hall.

“I said to you guys, we are going to turn Piddington, this small village, into the largest village on this earth,” Mr. McNally, the chair of the parish council, said on a Tuesday night in late September. “That we are going to put it on the map.”

And they had.

The village of just over 350 people voted on Sept. 15 to become independent of the United Kingdom, in protest against a government plan to house 1,250 male asylum seekers in a nearby former military site.

Piddington has not, in fact, broken away from the United Kingdom, as the referendum had no legal basis. But it catapulted the rural village in Oxfordshire to the top of news sites and social media feeds, a publicity coup that Mr. McNally likened to a “blueprint” for other places facing the possible arrival of asylum seekers.

Piddington swiftly became an example of how a small place could challenge a national government over concerns that inhabitants felt were being ignored. In this case, how could a small village with no shops or pubs cope with more than a thousand unemployed men suddenly on its outskirts?

The campaign, which at times amplified far-right talking points about immigrants, also illustrated how divisive migration has become around Europe. In Britain, while asylum applications are down since a peak late last year, they remain consistently higher than the pre-2021 average.

The highly visible arrival of migrants crossing the English Channel, almost all of whom apply for asylum, has become a flashpoint, though these small boat arrivals have also declined since their highest level in 2022.

The Piddington vote underlined a dilemma confronting many European governments: Where should asylum seekers be housed as their applications are processed and anti-immigrant sentiment becomes more forceful and widespread?

Among the locals opposing the plan was Melise Witkin, 59, who said the proximity of the site to a village green, the Jubilee Reserve, was worrying.

“No one in their right mind is going to want to walk around the Jubilee worried that they might come down the road and there might be 20 of them,” Ms. Witkin, 59, said of asylum seekers. “They might be the loveliest, loveliest guys, but what if they’re not?”

That perceived threat to women and children from the arrival of many unemployed men was a focus of the village vote. In Britain, asylum seekers have been barred from working since the early 2000s, and the government has a legal obligation to provide accommodation while claims are processed.

The former military site, on the village outskirts, would house 18- to 65-year-old men, according to the proposals. They would be allowed to come and go during the day.

Rachel Marsh, 54, also opposes the plan, believing the location unsuitable and the militarized setup inhumane. But she was one of 26 residents who voted against independence, after becoming uncomfortable with the campaign’s tone.

“They have fallen for the fear rhetoric — hook, line, and sinker,” she said of some neighbors. She felt sad, she said, that misinformation about immigrants being disproportionately violent or criminal was being used “to whip people into this radicalized frenzy.” (While data is limited, researchers say there is little evidence that immigration has an impact on overall crime rates.)

The independence campaign’s Facebook account, which Mr. McNally and others run, shared an A.I.-generated animation that depicts an idyllic-looking village populated by white people, who appear terrified and dismayed as shirtless Black men march and leer at young girls, while men in turbans scare children out of a playground.

The campaign, and Mr. McNally specifically, tagged and thanked right-wing activists and figures such as Elon Musk, who has regularly used social media to attempt to influence British politics. In an interview, Mr. McNally said Mr. Musk’s resharing of a campaign post was a positive turning point.

“I thought, right, we’re definitely onto something here,” he said, adding that it helped push a “narrative” about the risks to the community. When asked about accusations that xenophobic and racist imagery was used in campaign videos, he said he did not create the clips. “I don’t see it as racism at all,” he said, adding, “It’s telling the story of Piddington and as far as I am concerned, that is an accurate representation.”

In Britain more broadly, anger over immigration has grown in recent years and protests against asylum seekers have become disruptive and at times violent.

In September, hundreds of anti-migrant demonstrators wearing balaclavas gathered in Portsmouth, in southern England, blocking port access for several hours. This week, another group clashed with the police in Gosport, a coastal town where migrants were brought ashore on a rescue boat.

The backlash over using military sites follows an earlier outcry over the use of hotels for asylum accommodation, by the previous Conservative government, to comply with social distancing rules. After the pandemic, the number of people crossing the English Channel in small boats to claim asylum rose rapidly, while the processing of claims slowed, leading to a large backlog that the Labour government has only partly cut.

Shabana Mahmood, Labour’s home secretary who is responsible for immigration policies, has embraced a hard-line approach in an effort to show the government has heard voters’ concerns. Using former military sites instead of hotels — to create the perception of a less generous and more controlled approach — is part of that.

But efforts to convert military sites can be costly, high-profile and polarizing, said Sunder Katwala, director of British Future, a research organization in London. They also give agitators a place to go, and create a situation where locals’ concerns appear to be ignored, he said.

“That’s the one thing we should be trying to do: separate out real concerns from agitation and stirring up trouble,” he said. “What we don’t want, I think, is to cross the wires, where the reasonable parish council meeting attendee is now in receipt of extreme conspiracy narratives from the very far right.”

There is little doubt that Piddington residents genuinely oppose the site. A separate initiative, Wrong Plan, Wrong Site, is mounting evidence-based legal challenges to the proposal. But it has taken a back seat to the independence campaign’s more provocative arguments.

“None of that balance was brought into the equation,” Ms. Marsh said. She added, however, that the Labour government’s failure to listen to concerns had created space for vitriolic voices, saying: “Labour’s refusal to engage with the people on this has handed it to the far right.”

She and her husband have lived in Piddington for two decades and raised their children here. She is originally from New Zealand, and her husband’s parents were from the Windrush generation of Caribbean people who migrated legally to Britain after World War II.

After Ms. Marsh was interviewed on the BBC on the day of the referendum, she and her family received an onslaught of online abuse. An anti-immigrant campaigner arrived at her home, filmed her and published the footage, showing her address. The clip was shared by far-right agitators, and she met with the police to discuss her safety.

Still, Ms. Marsh said it remained important to offer an alternative perspective. “I do think there is an agenda here to keep us divided,” she said.

Piddington has been here before. In 2001, a plan to develop asylum accommodation outside the village also drew intense opposition. It was scrapped when the government determined it wasn’t economically viable.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that the military site was being considered because voters had wanted people out of hotels.

“But I’ve heard what people are saying in Piddington and the other places affected,” he said. “I don’t ignore their concerns.”

In a statement, the Home Office said it plans to close asylum hotels and move people to alternative accommodation, including former military sites “designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.”

item.title: Labour Holds Off Green Party in Election for Starmer’s Former London Seat
item.description:
The Labour Party in Britain held onto the parliamentary seat vacated by former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, winning a special election in central London that was seen as an early test for Andy Burnham, Mr. Starmer’s successor.

Sagal Abdi-Wali, who is currently the Labour Party leader of the local Camden Council, defeated the Green Party hopeful and other candidates to retain the Holborn and St. Pancras seat for her party.

She won with 45 percent of the vote, according to results announced in the early hours of Friday morning.

Ms. Abdi-Wali, who was born in Somalia and came to Britain as a child refugee in the 1990s, campaigned for many of the same policies that Mr. Burnham laid out in a speech at the Labour conference last month.

“Opportunities for young people, ending rough sleeping on our streets, making things like water bills more affordable and a safe, secure home,” she wrote in a recent online article. “These are my big priorities for Camden. But most of all — I want to give you hope again.”

The victory, while expected, is a boost to Mr. Burnham, who took over as the country’s leader after helping to engineer Mr. Starmer’s ouster over the summer. Surveys suggest that Mr. Burnham is popular with the public, and under his leadership, the party is once more leading in national polls. But he faces the same fundamental challenges that his predecessor did: a sluggish economy, rising prices and government bond yields because of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, and not enough money to pay for all the competing priorities.

Ms. Abdi-Wali defeated, among others, Zack Polanski, the leader of Britain’s Green Party, who was seeking his own seat in Parliament. Mr. Polanski ended up with 33 percent of the vote.

Mr. Polanski’s party has been having more success in British politics recently, and he had hoped that a victory in the central London district would add to the sense of momentum for the movement he leads.

But his political success has been marred by several controversies in recent months. Over the weekend, a small group of Green Party activists voted at the party’s annual conference to declare that Zionism is racism, a move that infuriated many supporters of Israel.

The measure passed with just over 1,000 votes out of the 1,800 cast at the conference. The party has more than 230,000 members. Mr. Polanski did not vote for the measure, but he has refused to criticize it. Asked later by the BBC about the motion, he said: “If your Zionism is the displacement of the Palestinian people, then that is clearly racist, and I say that as a Jewish leader of a British political party.”

item.title: Malaysia Welcomes Myanmar’s Autocrat
item.description:
Over the past few months, he has traveled to Russia, China, India, Belarus, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Laos. Now, the leader of one of the world’s most repressive governments, U Min Aung Hlaing of Myanmar, is being feted by Malaysia, where he met on Thursday with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

The summit, in which the two sides discussed the repatriation of Myanmar asylum-seekers in Malaysia and investment opportunities in a war-torn Myanmar, was the latest sign of a remarkable makeover for Mr. Min Aung Hlaing. Five years ago, he presided over a military coup that plunged Myanmar into full-blown civil war and made the Southeast Asian nation a global outcast.

But after trading his military uniform for civilian clothes earlier this year, the onetime junta leader has been basking in international recognition. In public remarks on Thursday, Mr. Anwar declined to utter a single critical word about the reign of terror unleashed under Mr. Min Aung Hlaing’s rule.

“Now we have had excellent relations for a long time, but of course, recent developments have somewhat blocked that sort of progress, so I think our interest is, of course, to enhance this collaboration,” Mr. Anwar said, in a delicate description of the coup and its deadly aftermath.

Since taking the presidential post, Mr. Min Aung Hlaing has traveled to five countries in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN. But he is still officially banned from attending its summits, an international affirmation that he craves, Myanmar observers say.

Mr. Anwar gave a wink-wink acknowledgment of the Myanmar leader’s efforts to work himself back into ASEAN’s good graces.

“You will continue your policy to engage with all parties to avoid further escalation of violence, and of course, I welcome that and convey it to my colleagues not only here but also in ASEAN,” Mr. Anwar said.

In April, Mr. Min Aung Hlaing became president, following his retirement as army chief and a set of stage-managed elections that the military’s proxy party contested virtually unopposed. Since then, the military’s attacks on civilian nationwide have not abated. A.C.L.E.D., a conflict monitoring group, says that Myanmar is one of the most dangerous places on earth, the severity of its conflict outranked only by that in the Palestinian territories. Last week, at least 50 people were killed in a military airstrike on a market in western Myanmar.

The two-day visit to Malaysia marked a rare foray by Mr. Min Aung Hlaing, one of the world’s leading jailers of political prisoners, to a nation that regularly holds unfettered elections. Mr. Anwar himself spent nearly 11 years in prison for what are widely regarded as politically motivated convictions.

On Thursday, a “cooperation dialogue” after the two leaders’ 40-minute tête-à-tête was dominated by business discussions. Among those attending on the Malaysian side were the trade minister and the central bank head, as well as top figures representing the palm oil industry, a telecommunications conglomerate, private banks and the state-owned oil and natural gas company. Mr. Anwar said that year-on-year trade with Myanmar had increased more than 140 percent.

After the coup, major democracies placed financial sanctions on members of Myanmar’s military leadership, as well as on the cronies propping up the regime. But on Thursday, the Myanmar delegation in Putrajaya, the Malaysian administrative capital, was studded with businessmen and generals-turned-cabinet ministers who are the subjects of asset freezes, travel bans and other financial restrictions imposed by Western nations.

Myanmar’s economy, once buoyed by foreign investment during a brief reform period, has contracted sharply since the military takeover, a downturn that Mr. Min Aung Hlaing has blamed on foreign sanctions and rebel incursions. More than two-thirds of Myanmar’s population is impoverished or in danger of falling into poverty, according to a new report from the United Nations Development Program.

Mr. Anwar’s decision to welcome the Myanmar leader comes amid growing xenophobia toward migrants in Malaysia, which prompted his plan to deport people from Myanmar back home. On Thursday, he praised Mr. Min Aung Hlaing for his “candid manner and willingness to collaborate” on the mass repatriation.

“Very few, hardly any country, in my experience, are willing to accept this repatriation in a large, in large number, at their own expense, as you have shown in Myanmar,” Mr. Anwar said.

The first batch of about 1,470 people left Malaysia on a Myanmar Navy ship a day after the airstrike killed more than 50 people in the country’s western Rakhine State. Much of Rakhine is now in the hands of a rebel militia. The Myanmar government minister for Rakhine was part of the Malaysia delegation.

Among the first deportees was Ko Min Nyan Tun, who said that he had to sign a document absolving Malaysia of legal responsibility if the ship back faced any difficulties. The journey itself was comfortable, he said, with plentiful food and karaoke breaks, although his family was made to pay the Myanmar Navy for these luxuries. His dread grew when he returned to Myanmar, he said, because he was given signals that he would likely be drafted into the military.

Fear of conscription has led at least a million young people to flee Myanmar since the coup. More than half the country is now in the hands of armed rebel groups, and the military has made up for a soldier shortfall by drafting men to the age of 35 and women to 27.

Mr. Min Nyan Tun, 34, said he has now been deported three times from Malaysia. But he said he would head back there again, somehow.

“If I had to choose between being arrested again in Malaysia and being sent to the front line, I would choose going back to Malaysia,” he said. “I can’t go to the front line and give my life for the military regime.”

Hundreds of thousands of people from Myanmar are believed to be working menial jobs in Malaysia without documentation. Around 215,000 refugees or asylum seekers from Myanmar are registered in Malaysia with the United Nations refugee agency.

Before the coup, Malaysia, a Muslim-majority nation, absorbed a population of Rohingya, a Muslim ethnicity from Myanmar that has long suffered repression. Effectively stateless, waves of Rohingya were violently expelled from their homeland nearly a decade ago, an exodus that ranks as one of the fastest refugee outflows in recent history. A genocide case against Myanmar is underway at the International Court of Justice at The Hague, with a ruling expected in the coming months.

After the first repatriations on Sept. 30, Mr. Anwar said that no Rohingya had been sent to Myanmar. But the prime minister also said last month that he wants to expel the entire population of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia. The majority of them are Rohingya. Complicating matters, Mr. Min Aung Hlaing said on Thursday that Myanmar would only repatriate “those confirmed as Myanmar citizens.” His government does not consider Rohingya to be from Myanmar.

“The idea that the refugee flow will somehow end after a meeting between Anwar and Min Aung Hlaing is ignorance,” said Charles Santiago, the Malaysian co-chair of ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights. “The flow will end when the violence ends.”

Mr. Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Malaysia was capped by a state luncheon in which the guests feasted on lamb with mint and black pepper sauces, jumbo prawns in buttermilk and a cheese and passion fruit pudding, among other delights.

One in three people in Myanmar, the U.N. says, now does not have enough to eat.

item.title: Houthi Attacks on Saudi Airports Prompt Mass Cancellations
item.description:
Explosions rattled the Saudi capital, Riyadh, on Thursday as the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen claimed to have attacked the city’s international airport for the second time this week.

The kingdom has been left reeling, with the Saudi authorities saying on Wednesday that Houthi strikes on airports in Riyadh and Abha, a city in the south of the country, had killed three people and injured dozens more.

The attacks are the deadliest on Saudi Arabia since the war with the Houthis reignited in recent weeks and threaten to widen a conflict that has entangled multiple countries and strained energy markets. Oil prices rose sharply on Thursday, with Brent crude, the global benchmark, up more than 5 percent.

The instability snarled air traffic, with around one in four departures from Saudi airports and dozens of inbound flights canceled, according to data from the aviation analytics firm Cirium. The Lufthansa Group suspended flights to Riyadh up to Oct. 16, the company said. And Air India’s flights to the Saudi capital were also paused, according to the Indian Embassy there.

The Saudi authorities said on Thursday that they had intercepted two ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh and that fragments of munitions had fallen onto a children’s nursery and a medical clinic. It was unclear if there were any casualties.

A Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said in statements Thursday that the militia had targeted Riyadh’s international airport, another airport in Najran and a Saudi air base near Khamis Mushait in the country’s south. He said the missile attacks had struck a target at the Riyadh airport and disrupted air traffic, without elaborating.

The Saudi authorities did not respond to questions on the Houthis’ claims.

The New York Times has verified two videos circulating on social media that showed a thick plume of black smoke billowing over Riyadh’s airport, which has announced dozens of flight cancellations.

The targeting of Riyadh has raised pressure on Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, to resolve the escalating conflict as the fighting threatens his plans to turn the country into a business and tourism hub. Riyadh is set to host several international events in the coming weeks, including an annual investment summit hosted by Prince Mohammed that is typically attended by world leaders, billionaires and top global executives.

Saudi Arabia announced a new bombing campaign in Yemen this week against the Houthis, who have vowed to fight back by hitting airports and energy infrastructure.

Prince Mohammed has also sought to secure greater military support from allies, including the United States, which is providing significant assistance to the kingdom’s bombing campaign.

The fighting could entangle more parties, after Pakistan and Turkey this week activated a defense pact to provide military support to Saudi Arabia. A senior Pakistani military official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, said on Wednesday that Pakistani fighter jets were being used in strikes against the Houthis.

It was unclear if foreign military intervention would temper attacks by the Houthis, who have survived years of bombing campaigns and have calculated that they can inflict greater pain on Saudi Arabia than the kingdom can on them.

A Times reporter in Riyadh heard several blasts in quick succession on Thursday morning. Two residents, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said workers at an office tower in the city had been told to evacuate. In recent days, the Saudi authorities have told residents not to share information related to missile and drone attacks, warning them of legal consequences.

The Houthis say that their attacks in Saudi Arabia are retaliation for attacks in Yemen.

The conflict in Yemen is being fought on multiple fronts. The internationally recognized government of Yemen, backed by Saudi warplanes, began a counteroffensive this week to retake strategically important territory along the Red Sea from the Houthis. The militia seized parts of the coast last month in a move that gave it greater control over the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical global trade route.

The Houthis say they have made gains in the inland city of Taiz, a government stronghold.

A Yemeni government army officer in Taiz said that Houthi forces had effectively encircled the city and that residents were running out of gas and food supplies. He spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorized to speak to the media.

A spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, said overnight that it had attacked dozens of Houthi military sites, including missile storage facilities and command centers, in retaliation for the airport strikes on Wednesday. The Houthis did not respond to that claim.

The latest round of fighting has plunged Saudi Arabia and the Houthis back into open conflict, and nearly 200,000 Yemenis have been displaced since September, when the fighting intensified, according to the United Nations.

In 2015, Saudi Arabia led a disastrous campaign against the Houthis in a bid to restore Yemen’s government, which had been driven out of the capital, Sanaa, by the militia.

The war led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, until the two sides agreed to a tenuous truce in 2022.

Senator Chris Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut, who met with Prince Mohammed on Monday in Riyadh and publicly opposed the kingdom’s last campaign in Yemen, said that it was unclear what the kingdom’s long-term objectives are in its renewed military campaign.

“They want to win back the territory that they’ve lost, and I think the open question is whether they have clear goals beyond that,” Mr. Murphy told reporters. “I think history tells us that this military conflict, whoever starts it, is a disaster for the people of Yemen, for the region, and for the United States.”

Analysts said the attacks on Riyadh in recent days would make it more likely that the Saudi government would intensify its bombing campaign in Yemen.

“The latest attack just gives them more international support for any military operation they would do against the Houthis,” said Farea al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at Chatham House, a London-based research group.

President Trump has rebuffed Saudi government requests to direct American airstrikes. But more than 200 U.S. intelligence and military analysts are assisting the Saudi government in command centers inside the kingdom, helping to analyze and select targets in support of its Yemeni allies, according to one current and one former U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters. The United States is also providing aerial refueling for Saudi warplanes conducting defensive air patrols, they added.

Last month, Britain also promised to offer limited aerial refueling to Saudi warplanes for defensive purposes. It is unclear if that will extend to the new campaign. France said last month that it would send troops and other military assets to protect Saudi energy infrastructure on the Red Sea.

Saeed Al-Batati contributed reporting from al-Mukalla, Yemen, and Pranav Baskar contributed reporting from New York.

item.title: Margaret Papandreou, American-Born First Lady of Greece, Dies at 102
item.description:
Margaret Papandreou, who helped transform legal and social rights for Greek women in the 1980s as the American-born wife of Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou and who later supported feminist and socialist movements around the world, died on Sept. 18 at her home in Palaio Faliro, a seaside suburb of Athens. She was 102.

Her family announced the death.

Ms. Papandreou’s tireless organizing and her direct pipeline to power were credited with spurring fundamental shifts in Greece that included legalizing abortion and removing antiquated social codes, such as requiring a husband’s permission for a woman to start a business or travel abroad with their children.

“The women’s movement is a political movement,” she said at a United Nations conference on women in Nairobi, Kenya, in 1985. “It is a social revolution. It is about changes in society, changes that are global.”

After a bitter public divorce in 1989, she expanded her role in international efforts to promote women in politics and retained prominence in Greece as matriarch of the third generation in a left-leaning political dynasty. Her son George A. Papandreou (pronounced Pap-an-DREY-oo) served as prime minister from 2009 to 2011.

With an easy smile and Midwestern openness that confused and charmed Greeks, Ms. Papandreou set the foundation for her influence in women’s issues during the heady era after the collapse of a seven-year military junta in 1974.

The Papandreous had fled from the junta’s crackdowns on dissent and were back from a self-exile in northern Europe and Canada, where Ms. Papandreou wrote a memoir, “Nightmare in Athens” (1970), recounting the events as dictatorship began in 1967. With the return of democracy, her husband’s Panhellenic Socialist Movement, or Pasok, was surging in strength.

Ms. Papandreou, who was known as Margarita in Greece, borrowed from the party’s populist-style tactics. She traveled across cities and rural areas to meet with women to discuss their aspirations and concerns, which at the time included the age-old system of the bride’s family providing a dowry before marriage. (It wasn’t until 1952 that Greek women could vote in national elections.)

Her efforts coalesced around the Women’s Union of Greece, a group she founded in 1975 and led for eight years. Opposition came from many directions. The Greek Orthodox Church claimed that Ms. Papandreou was undermining cultural traditions. Right-wing newspapers painted her as an interloper and made note of her American-accented Greek.

But national elections in 1981 gave Pasok a landslide victory and made her husband prime minister. “We’ve had enough of being second-class citizens, always pushed to the margin,” Ms. Papandreou said to a crowd of female voters at a pre-election rally for the Greek actress, singer and political activist Melina Mercouri, who was her husband’s ally. Ms. Mercouri won a seat in Parliament and was named culture minister.

We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

Using the clout of her first lady status, Ms. Papandreou lobbied Pasok members in Parliament to act quickly on legislation to dismantle the restrictions on women.

Her crowning moment came in 1983 with the passage of a sweeping law that effectively gave women equal status on domestic issues and ended any lingering male-permission rules. The reforms also abolished dowries, created divorce by mutual consent and made single mothers the legal guardians of their children. In another first, women no longer had to change their names after marriage.

In 1986, Greece legalized abortion, making it one of the last Western European countries to end widespread restrictions — although some countries, including Poland and Malta, still maintain strict abortion regulations.

In a statement from President Constantine Tassoulas of Greece after Ms. Papandreou’s death, he described her as a cornerstone for “the reform of family law, the breakthrough in social and political rights, and the modernization of women’s status in Greek society.”

Apart from her political achievements, Ms. Papandreou’s legacy was also intertwined with modern Greece’s most watched breakup drama.

In a spectacle that played out in the press, she endured humiliation and responded with scorn after her husband of nearly 40 years and father of her four adult children started a relationship with Dimitra Liani, an Olympic Airways flight attendant who was half his age.

By the late 1980s, Ms. Liani had become the de facto first lady. She appeared with the prime minister during visits by dignitaries and at international events. In 1988, Ms. Liani and the prime minister were photographed walking hand in hand on the grounds of Harefield Hospital outside London, where he underwent heart surgery. Ms. Papandreou refused to visit him.

At first, Ms. Papandreou said she would not agree to a divorce, but she signed the papers in June 1989. The next month, just after finishing his second term, Mr. Papandreou, then 70, and Ms. Liani married. He was back in office from 1993 to 1996, resigning months before his death.

During Ms. Papandreou’s marital ordeal, public sympathy largely flowed to her because of how the prime minister flaunted his extramarital relationship in public.

“I refuse to be the victim,” Ms. Papandreou told The New York Times in 1989. “I believe I will come out of this very strong. Maybe I’ll come out of it the stronger of the two.”

Margaret Esther Chant, the oldest of five sisters, was born in Oak Park, Ill., on Sept. 30, 1923, and raised in nearby Elmhurst, west of Chicago. Her mother, Hulda (Pfund) Chant, was a homemaker, and her father, Douglas Chant, was a car mechanic who lost his job during the Great Depression.

The family’s financial struggles left a deep imprint on Margaret’s views on social justice.

“It seemed to me that there was something very unjust about people having a lot of money while others had none,” she later told The Washington Post. “The principles of socialism appealed to me. They were human goals, health, education, a right to work.”

At the University of Minnesota, she received a bachelor’s degree in journalism in 1946 and a master’s degree in public health in 1950. During her postgraduate studies, she started a small public relations firm in Minneapolis and struck a side deal to help a local dentist write his autobiography in exchange for free dental care.

While in the waiting room at the dentist’s office in 1948, she met Andreas Papandreou, an associate professor of economics at her alma mater and the son of a former Greek prime minister, George Papandreou, one of the pro-Western power brokers as Greece descended into factional fighting after World War II.

“By the end of that evening, I was in love with him,” she recalled to The Minneapolis Star Tribune in 1996. He was married at the time, and she was later briefly married to Robert L. Hall, a doctoral student in sociology. After their divorces, they wed each other in 1951.

Mr. Papandreou became chairman of the economics department at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1955, but he harbored ambitions as political heir to his father, and the couple relocated to Athens in 1961.

Mr. Papandreou’s political rise was soon underway after his father regained the prime minister post in the mid-1960s, a period of political upheavals when military commanders began plotting the coup. Ms. Papandreou came to wider notice to the Greek public in the coup’s aftermath as the junta rounded up left-leaning political leaders, students, intellectuals and others, including her husband.

She aggressively campaigned for his release, enlisting prominent friends like the economist and former U.S. diplomat John Kenneth Galbraith. After Mr. Papandreou was freed in 1968, the family left the country and eventually settled in Canada.

From their self-exile, Ms. Papandreou and her husband were increasingly dismayed by U.S. aid to the junta, which was seen by Washington as an anti-communist bulwark despite the regime’s repression and human rights violations.

For decades after, Ms. Papandreou and her husband remained sharp critics of U.S. policies, calling for the removal of military bases in Greece and describing unfettered capitalism as “anti-feminist.”

“I don’t hate the people there, or even the government,” she told The Globe and Mail of Toronto in 1983. “I just think it’s on the wrong track, that it neglects the interests of poor and oppressed people. But it would be nonsense to deny my past, my culture.”

In addition to her son George A. Papandreou, survivors include two other sons, Andreas Papandreou and Nikos Papandreou, a member of the European Parliament; a daughter, Sofia Papandreou; six grandchildren; and a great-granddaughter.

In 2015, Ms. Papandreou published a second memoir, “Love and Power: A Midwestern First Lady.” In speeches and interviews, she recounted being asked whether she ever dreamed she would become the wife of Greece’s prime minister.

“No,” she liked to say. “I dreamed I would grow up to be the prime minister of Greece.”

item.title: Escalating Assaults on Ukrainian Cities Are Taking an Enormous Toll
item.description:
It was a devastating scene in a devastated city.

Under shredded netting meant to shield civilians from Russian drones, near residential buildings shattered by explosions, the charred metal skeleton of a commuter bus was all that was left on Thursday after another Russian strike in Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.

At least 30 people were killed, local officials said, the latest civilian casualties in Moscow’s unrelenting campaign to make Ukraine’s towns and cities unlivable.

As rescue workers in Kramatorsk were tending to the injured and gathering body parts from the street, President Volodymyr Zelensky was making his way to another Ukrainian city, Pryluky, where he implored the world to do more to counter Russian aggression.

He stood near the rubble of an apartment building destroyed by a Russian missile on Wednesday, killing 22 people, including five children. Entire families died in that strike.

Speaking in Pryluky, which was hit despite being about 200 miles from any combat zone, Mr. Zelensky said that Russia was seeking ways to expand its advantage in the skies and unleash more terror.

He warned that China was developing technology meant to compete with the Starlink satellite network and planned to share it with Russia. He called on the United States to allow Ukraine to use Starlink to target Russian missile and drone launch sites inside Russia.

The price of inaction, Mr. Zelensky said, was scenes like those in Pryluky, where he met with rescue workers and grieving families.

The Russian military has attacked civilian homes throughout the war. But the death toll is rising as Moscow fields an ever-growing supply of powerful precision weapons, stretching Ukraine’s air defenses with daily onslaughts.

The Kremlin has expanded its arsenal of newly developed jet-powered drones and increased the range of powerful guided bombs dropped from warplanes. Russia is also employing new communication tools that allow pilots to remotely guide munitions for precision strikes from hundreds of miles away.

Russia launched about 3,500 jet-powered drones against targets across Ukraine in September, compared with 350 in June, according to the Ukrainian Air Force. Ukraine is working furiously to develop interceptors that work against the jet-powered drones, which travel hundreds of miles per hour.

On Thursday morning, one of those jet drones smashed into a store in downtown Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, killing three people and injuring 14 others, city officials said.

The store was hit a day after a large-scale bombardment on Wednesday killed at least 30 people across the country, including six in the capital.

Mr. Zelensky noted that the bombardment, which included the cruise missile strike on the apartment complex in Pryluky, coincided with President Vladimir V. Putin’s 74th birthday.

“This is the kind of ‘gift’ Putin gave himself for his birthday,” Mr. Zelensky said on Wednesday. “The killing of children, the killing of people.”

While drones and missiles pose the biggest threat across Ukraine, frontline cities like Kramatorsk, where the bus was struck, are being slowly destroyed by artillery and guided bombs that can pack hundreds of pounds of explosives.

In August, Russia dropped a record 8,700 guided bombs on military and civilian targets, according to the Ukrainian military. The only reliable defense against these bombs, which can hit targets more than 100 miles from where they are released, is to take out the warplanes that deliver them or destroy the warehouses where they are stored.

The epicenter of the fighting remains the eastern Donetsk region, where the majority of glide bomb strikes are recorded. Ukraine still controls around 20 percent of the territory, including Kramatorsk, Sloviansk and other cities that make up a belt of heavily fortified land.

Around 93,000 civilians remain in areas under Ukrainian control in Donetsk, including more than 4,200 children, according to local officials.

“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” Vadym Filashkin, the head of the Donetsk regional military administration, said in a statement after the attack on the bus. “For them, a bus carrying passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.”

Nataliia Novosolova and Liubov Sholudko contributed reporting.

item.description:
China has begun operating a new air force base in Laos, marking another step in Beijing’s efforts to establish military footholds abroad and project power into Southeast Asia.

Satellite images released this week revealed that eight small military aircraft had arrived at the China-Laos Joint Logistics and Training Center, which officially opened late last month at Ban Keun, about 30 miles north of the Laotian capital, Vientiane.

The satellite images, first reported by Reuters, showed a 1.2-mile runway at Ban Keun that could be extended, opening the possibility that the facility could host bigger aircraft that need longer takeoffs and landings.

The base in Laos, a landlocked country between Vietnam and Thailand, could help the Chinese air force reach across the region, including countries with which Beijing has long-running territorial tensions over the South China Sea, some experts said.

China has the world’s second biggest military after the United States. The People’s Liberation Army has been expanding rapidly but has taken limited only steps to open bases in other countries: a naval facility in Cambodia and another naval support center in Djibouti, in East Africa.

“Ban Keun is significant because it appears to be China’s first openly acknowledged overseas military facility for air power,” said Ying Yu Lin, an associate professor at Tamkang University in Taipei who studies China’s military. The new facility “sits in the center of the Indochinese peninsula, and could enable the Chinese Communist Party to easily project air power across surrounding areas.”

But for now at least, the Chinese air force presence at Ban Keun is too small and isolated to have tangible military consequences, said Drew Thompson, a former Pentagon official.

“Laos is landlocked, so a base there doesn’t give the Lao or Chinese air force unfettered access to the Indian Ocean or Gulf of Thailand,” said Mr. Thompson, who is now a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. “The threat of a joint Lao-China air force base is primarily political rather than military because it was established without consultation” with Laos’ neighbors.

The eight aircraft at Ban Keun were possibly K-8 jets, also called Hongdu JL-8, a light two-seater built by China and Pakistan that is mostly used for training, said Professor Lin. Laos’ air force has only a few dozen aircraft, including about four of the K-8 jets, according to an annual global military survey from the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

Nearby countries such as Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore will likely watch to see if Ban Keun’s runway is lengthened to host bombers or surveillance aircraft. Many Chinese fighter jets and other aircraft can take off from runways shorter than the one at Ban Keun, but standard Chinese air force runways are often notably longer.

Countries in Southeast Asia generally try to stay friendly with Beijing, while many also look to the United States to counterbalance Chinese power. Singapore and Thailand, in particular, provide logistic support for U.S. forces in the region, said Professor Lin. Vietnam, which has had acrimonious boundary disputes with China, has also turned to the United States.

Rear Admiral Surasant Kongsiri, a spokesman for Thailand’s Ministry of Defense, said Laos had the right to decide whether to allow China to operate a base there, Reuters reported. “Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments,” he said.

Ban Keun has been used by a foreign military before. During the Vietnam War, an airfield there served as a forward base for covert American support operations that were carried out under the name Air America.

Construction on the new base began around October 2025 and proceeded swiftly, satellite images show. By May, much of the runway was visible.

In late September, Laotian and Chinese military officers assembled for the formal opening of the support and training center, a Chinese television report showed. China’s Ministry of National Defense said that Ban Keun was “not aimed at any third party.”

The center will be “jointly maintained by both sides” and “its construction and operation are the fruit of mutual respect and consultation on an equal basis between China and Laos,” the ministry said.

In recent decades, Laos has increasingly depended on China for investment, political support and tourism.

In January, the International Monetary Fund warned that Laos, one of Asia’s poorest and least developed nations, has a debt burden that is “unsustainable.” About half of Laos’ public debt is owed to China, which has financed a high-speed railway that largely bypasses the local population. Laos has also poured money into hydropower, and a Chinese joint venture now runs its power grid.

China’s first major military foothold in Southeast Asia was at a naval base in Ream, Cambodia, which it helped expand into a deepwater base. Cambodia has lately tried to reduce its reliance on China by courting Washington, both by lauding President Donald Trump and welcoming a visit in January by an American warship.

item.title: Nana Patekar, Indian Actor Who Embodied the Everyman, Dies at 75
item.description:
Nana Patekar, an Indian actor who became a star playing the Everyman but also was a figure in India’s fleeting #MeToo reckoning, died on Thursday in the state of Goa. He was 75.

The cause was cardiac arrest, Dr. Shekhar Salkar, a physician at Manipal Hospitals in Goa, told journalists. Mr. Patekar’s caretaker found him unconscious in his apartment in Panaji, the state capital, early on Thursday, Dr. Salkar said.

A theater actor who brought intensity and a coarse baritone to the screen, Mr. Patekar was a star in Hindi and Marathi films, with credits including Mira Nair’s “Salaam Bombay!” (“Greetings to Bombay!”) in 1988. He was one of the few actors to win awards for best actor, supporting actor and villain at India’s Filmfare Awards. His career also showcased how male actors escaped relatively unscathed from India’s #MeToo movement.

“He brought remarkable diversity and creativity to every role, creating characters that will remain in the memory of generations,” Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India said in a social media tribute.

In 2008, Tanushree Dutta, a Bollywood actress and former Miss India, said that Mr. Patekar had ordered changes to a dance sequence so that he could grope her on a film set. Ms. Dutta fled the set, but a mob later surrounded her car, smashed the windshield, flattened the tires and trapped her inside. Footage of the incident aired on Indian television, and Ms. Dutta continued to speak out. She filed a police complaint against Mr. Patekar, who denied the allegations.

We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

Nothing came of it until a decade later, when Ms. Dutta revived her complaint as the #MeToo movement spread to India and other women began voicing accusations about prominent men. A witness corroborated her account, and other actors spoke out in support. Ms. Dutta filed a new complaint with the police in 2018, but they cleared Mr. Patekar in 2019, saying investigators had found no evidence to support the complaint. Mr. Patekar’s career quickly rebounded, but Ms. Dutta’s sputtered.

Ms. Dutta released a video statement on Thursday amid an outpouring of grief in India over Mr. Patekar’s death. “I’m worried that in the evening, that’s all the media’s going to be interested in is evil dead,” she said. She said she would speak “once I figure out what kind of reaction I should have” and added, “Condolences to the family.”

Vishwanath Patekar was born in 1951 in Murud Janjira, a village near the coastal town of Alibag in India’s western state of Maharashtra. As a child, his mother’s close friend called him Nana, and the name stuck. His family fell into poverty after his father, a textile merchant, lost his business and his property, Mr. Patekar said in a 2015 interview with the Times of India.

At 13, he got a job painting film posters. At school, he fell in love with the theater, and he went on to study at the Sir J. J. School of Art, Architecture and Design in Mumbai.

His first film role was in 1978 in “Gaman” (“Departure”), about migrants trying to build better lives in Mumbai. After a brief stint in advertising, a fellow actress took him along to a film audition where he turned down “a lousy role of one of the rapists,” he told The Times of India in 2015. Instead, he said, he landed a role that would get him noticed, in the 1984 film “Aaj Ki Awaaz” (“Voice of the Day”).

At 27, he married Neelakanti, a theater actress who supported them through her work in a bank, he told The Times of India. The couple had a son, Durvasa, who died at age 2, and later another son, Malhar. Ms. Patekar wrote and directed a Marathi film and returned fully to acting in the 2025 historical TV drama “Chhaava” (“Lion Cub”).

Mr. Patekar’s wife and son survive him. Full information on his survivors was not available.

Mr. Patekar’s career took off in 1989 with “Parinda” (“Bird”). His portrayal of a Mumbai gangster earned him his first National Film Award for best supporting actor. A year earlier, he starred in “Salaam Bombay!,” which won the Camera d’Or prize for best first feature at the Cannes Film Festival. He won another National Film Award in 1994, this time for best actor for his role as a disillusioned drifter turned activist in “Krantiveer” (“Brave Revolutionary”).

In the 2007 film “Welcome,” he played with the gangster archetype, creating one of his most popular comic characters — a gangster less interested in violence than in finding a suitable husband for his sister.

His characters were often men who felt thwarted — by bureaucracy, poverty, crime, family or the state. The roles gave form to a kind of middle-class frustration that was seldom the stuff of conventional Bollywood stardom. With his signature gravelly baritone, he was lauded by critics for his vulnerability on camera and his willingness to play frustrated or compromised men.

Mr. Patekar was also known for his outspoken political voice, and Mr. Modi praised him for his “forthright views.” He also worked with rural communities in his home province, raising funds for farmers facing drought.

item.title: Warrants to Search Former Prince Andrew’s Properties Were Unlawful, Court Says
item.description:
Warrants used by the police to search two properties linked to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, were unlawful, a judge in London said on Thursday.

The judge, Nicholas Hilliard, told the courtroom that the police force responsible for the searches had agreed that a “significant error was made in the application for and the granting of the search warrants” but added that the material collected during those searches might ultimately be retained by the police.

“The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring an investigation to an end, or mean that the whole of the investigation was unlawful,” Judge Hilliard said.

Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor, the younger brother of King Charles III, was arrested on Feb. 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office over accusations that he had shared confidential information with Jeffrey Epstein.

Two properties associated with Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor, including his former residence at Royal Lodge in Windsor and another property on the king’s Sandringham Estate, were searched. Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor was later released without charge and has denied wrongdoing.

The judge said that the police obtained documentary material and electronic devices during the searches of the properties.

During the court hearing on Thursday, it was revealed that Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor had first filed a legal action challenging the search warrants in May. By July 22, the police had agreed they were unlawful, and the High Court quashed them.

However a privacy order, requested by the police while other legal challenges continue over whether it can retain the evidence it collected, prevented the information from being made public until Thursday.

For now, any evidence collected will remain in police custody, the judge said.

A court hearing will be held in 2027 to determine whether the police can continue to retain the property that was seized under the unlawful warrants. Under British law, the police can apply to the court to keep material if they have grounds to immediately seize evidence again using a lawful warrant.

The Thames Valley Police, the police force responsible for conducting the investigation into Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor, had applied for search warrants during a private hearing at England’s Central Criminal Court on Feb. 18, 2026, a day before Mr. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested and his properties searched.

In a statement, the police force said that the quashing of the warrants “relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation.”

It said that it had “ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout,” but it accepted that the initial court’s decision to issue the warrants under a “specific piece of legislation” was incorrect.

item.title: Russia’s Vague Account of a Mysterious Death Is Stoking Cover-Up Fears
item.description:
As rumors swirled this week that a woman working in a Siberian lab may have died of the plague, news programs on Russian state television paid scant attention. The authorities in Moscow released little information.

Faced with this potential new threat, the Kremlin seems to be resorting to a familiar playbook: avoiding bad news.

The lack of information has caused unease around the world, particularly given the memory of China’s effort to withhold information about Covid-19.

In Russia, federal officials are generally reluctant, even fearful, about publishing anything that might cast the Kremlin in a negative light. The pace of news in Russia tends to be determined by the government, not by when events actually occur. The independent press has been driven into exile.

Perhaps the most notorious case was the hidden news that an explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear plant in April 1986 had contaminated a wide area with dangerous radiation. The Kremlin began to release information only after Sweden and other European countries, alarmed by high radiation readings, demanded an explanation.

In 1979, there was an accidental leak of anthrax spores from a secret biological weapon facility run by the Soviet military near what is now Yekaterinburg. Someone turned on a machine that dried the spores without realizing that a maintenance technician had removed a clogged exhaust filter.

More than 60 people died, as well as countless farm animals downwind of the facility. The Soviet authorities blamed the human toll on tainted meat, and the truth did not emerge until 1992, after the Soviet Union collapsed.

But the obfuscation did not stop, especially after Vladimir V. Putin became president in 2000.

In two of the most tragic episodes, the government either concealed the truth or promoted outright falsehoods. One was the sinking of the Kursk nuclear-powered submarine in the Barents Sea in 2000, with all 118 sailors aboard killed. In 2002, Chechen terrorists took over 900 people hostage during a performance of the “Nord-Ost” musical. Interior Ministry special forces knocked everybody out by pumping a chemical agent into the theater. But they failed to coordinate with the medical services, leading to the deaths of at least 116 hostages, as well as all 41 attackers.

Since Russian forces mounted a large-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, there have been examples of the government’s effort to camouflage the true scope of the war.

Earlier this year, when a bomb exploded in a Moscow restaurant where a top Russian general was celebrating, Russian state news initially reported it as a gas canister explosion. The Kremlin has resorted to extensive censorship to hide Russian losses in its war in Ukraine — which the government made illegal to call a war. Independent researchers have estimated that 450,000 Russian soldiers have died.

Although several state-run newspapers initially ran articles about the death in Siberia, the news disappeared from their websites.

Alexandra Arkhipova, a Russian anthropologist in exile, wrote on social media, “Instead of a straightforward description of what is happening in Irkutsk, news columns are filled with journalistic euphemisms — clearly by order from above.”

There is no mention of plague, she added, only headlines about the “Irkutsk infection,” referring to the region of Siberia where the woman, who was 28, died.

Local social media accounts are full of questions and concerns about the case, although the occasional comment reflects the official line that people should rely on government statements.

Alyona, reached via social media and identified by only one name to avoid retribution from the authorities, said she was an old school friend of the victim but had not been in touch for a long time. “Everyone is worried, especially since there have been no clear statements,” she said.

The mystery surrounding the death in Irkutsk deepened because the governor of a neighboring region had initially posted on social media that the woman had died of the plague, and then changed it later to say that she had “possibly” died of the plague.

Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, criticized the news media for reporting rumors rather than relying on official reports from the public health safety agency. Even though the agency’s head, a doctor, flew to Irkutsk to assess the situation, it avoids news conferences, communicating only by intermittent press releases.

Russia’s public health agency has said the pathogen that killed the woman was not the one she had been researching in the lab, for which she had been vaccinated.

On Thursday, the governor of Irkutsk, Igor Kobzev, who has been posting regularly on his social media channels, wrote that all preventive measures had been completed and after about 5,000 laboratory tests, nobody else the victim might have been in contact with at the institute or the hospital was infected. “Amid intense media scrutiny, the specialists ​thoroughly investigated the situation,” he wrote. “It was a test, but we passed it in worthy fashion.”

His post attracted comments from area residents asking for a clearer explanation of what exactly had happened and what had killed the woman.

Russian officials have said the lab worker in Siberia died from pneumonia, of an unknown cause, on Friday night. Although the World Health Organization sent an initial query, the Russian authorities did not provide an answer in the required 24 hours, but three days later, the organization said.

The W.H.O. said Russia had not yet provided the details needed to make a formal “risk assessment” about the disease’s possible spread. Senior officials in both the E.U. and the United States, including President Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, all encouraged Russia to provide more information.

From 2019 to 2025, 10 countries reported almost 4,000 plague cases and 423 deaths, according to W.H.O. statistics. The United States reports about seven cases annually — the most recent was a woman in her 50s who died in June in New Mexico. Plague can be successfully treated with antibiotics if caught early.

Wrestling with the Covid pandemic, which completely disrupted ordinary life, left a legacy of mistrust toward public health agencies and their ability to protect people.

At a news conference on Wednesday, Maria Van Kerkhove, director of epidemic and pandemic management at the W.H.O., said, “Covid is certainly in the back of everybody’s mind.”

“If this individual did not die from the plague, then how did she die?” Dr. Van Kerkhove asked, adding, “We expect further answers from Russia.”

Alina Lobzina, Ivan Nechepurenko, Paul Sonne and Milana Mazaeva contributed reporting.

item.title: 2 Latvians Arrested After Breaching Perimeter of British Air Base Used by U.S.
item.description:
Two Latvian men were arrested Thursday inside the perimeter of a British air base used by the United States and are being investigated on suspicion of a national security offense, according to counterterrorism police.

The two men, aged 36 and 32, are Latvian citizens living in Britain, according to the police statement. They were arrested at around 2 a.m. on Thursday after being discovered inside the perimeter of the base, R.A.F. Molesworth, about 70 miles north of London, in Cambridgeshire.

Their ability to enter the base will underline concerns about security at military installations operated by the United States inside Britain and other countries, which have been on heightened alert after officials in Britain, the United States, Israel and Germany received evidence of threats against the bases from Iran.

Last month, five British men were arrested on suspicion of a plot targeting R.A.F. Fairford, the air base used by United States bombers in some strikes against Iran during their eight-month war, although they have not been charged and the details of the incident remain murky.

The British police said Thursday that they do not believe that the arrests at R.A.F. Molesworth, which is about two hours north of London, are connected to the incident at Fairford.

“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at R.A.F. Fairford last week,” said Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, in the statement. She added: “A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage.”

In Fairford, the five men arrested on Sept. 27 were released on bail the next day. Since then, two more men have been arrested in connection with the case and later freed on bail, including one man who was released on Thursday.

The police said that the investigation at Molesworth began at around 10 p.m. on Wednesday, when security patrols from the ministry of defense police found an abandoned vehicle just outside the perimeter of the base.

Additional police officers arrived and a “small breach” of the perimeter fence was discovered. The two Latvian men were located and arrested inside the perimeter at around 2 a.m., the statement said.

The men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing, but they were subsequently rearrested on suspicion of a national security offense, “namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the U.K.,” the police said.

After the abandoned vehicle was taken to a police location, a specialist explosives team was deployed to carry out checks on the vehicle and a cordon in the area was put in place. The explosives team ultimately found nothing of concern, the police said.

Both men remain in custody.

U.S. European Command said in a statement it would not discuss “specific force protection measures” but said it continued to “assess the threat environment surrounding our installations and take appropriate actions to protect our people, our platforms, and the bases where our forces operate from.”

The statement added: “We would also express our gratitude to the U.K. for the close partnership with U.S. Forces on matters of security.”

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: How a U.S. Diplomat Suppressed and Altered Reports Critical of Israel
item.description:
In late March, at the height of the Iran war, Israel quietly approved more settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank than it ever had at one time.

Staff members at the United States Embassy in Jerusalem saw the move as potentially flouting one of President Trump’s explicit red lines for Israel — no annexation of the West Bank — and drafted an urgent report intended for policy makers in Washington.

That memo never reached Washington. It was quashed by David Milstein, a top aide to Ambassador Mike Huckabee, according to three U.S. officials briefed on the process.

This was no isolated incident.

Since taking up his post in April 2025, Mr. Milstein, 36, has repeatedly suppressed or significantly revised embassy reporting on Israeli activities to present the Netanyahu government in a favorable light, according to a dozen people who work with or interact with Mr. Milstein in both Jerusalem and Washington:

As settler violence in the West Bank surged in the spring, for instance, he stymied embassy reporting suggesting that the Israeli government was failing to take action, according to the three officials. Instead the embassy sent a cable to Washington, viewed by The New York Times, praising Israel for “cracking down” on the attacks.

When members of Congress pushed for accountability over the killings of Palestinian Americans by Israeli settlers and security forces, he suppressed a detailed report that the embassy staff had written, effectively stonewalling lawmakers’ efforts to gain information, according to multiple officials briefed on the matter.

Soon after arriving in Jerusalem, Mr. Milstein began insisting on approving communications from the embassy section that handles Palestinian affairs, multiple officials with direct knowledge of the process said. The flow of cables plummeted from several a week to a few a month, as some staffers refrained from writing reports for fear that Mr. Milstein would block or rewrite them, these officials said.

Mr. Milstein’s interventions go far beyond those of any recent predecessor, several officials said. They and others said they were speaking out of concern that officials in Washington were getting a distorted view of Israeli actions through core diplomatic channels.

Mr. Milstein’s efforts have helped insulate Israel’s right-wing government against potential blowback from a Trump Administration that has been its closest ally.

Among the most contentious issues on which Mr. Milstein has intervened is the accelerating expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

It’s an inflammatory subject that has soured Israel’s relationship with some of its longtime allies. Last month, Britain, Canada and France announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank in response to the Israeli policy on settlement expansion. Britain accused some settlers of “ethnic cleansing.”

It is unclear to what extent Mr. Huckabee is aware of his adviser’s actions. Both he and Mr. Milstein declined requests for an interview.

The ambassador, a longtime advocate for the Israeli settlement movement, has denounced specific attacks by settlers, calling them “Israeli terrorists,” but he has played down settler violence more broadly, saying it is being carried out by a small group.

Mr. Huckabee is required to sign off on most cables and significant decisions, but officials said Mr. Milstein sometimes acts on his own. The ambassador has also sometimes worked in concert with Mr. Milstein to suppress or recast information, these officials said. But in several cases when he believed Mr. Milstein had gone too far, they said, Mr. Huckabee has reined him in.

Earlier this month, after an article critical of Mr. Milstein for inviting wedding guests to give him money appeared in Politico, Mr. Huckabee posted on social media that he had “absolute confidence” in his aide, whom he said possesses “impeccable integrity.”

Mr. Milstein is a familiar figure in right-wing circles in the United States and Israel, and has organized meetings between Mr. Huckabee and some top Israeli officials. But he is not well known in either country, and his role as a gatekeeper of information sent to Washington has drawn little attention.

His effort to shape embassy reporting was first reported a year ago by the online magazine of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a Washington think tank that advocates de-escalation and U.S. military restraint.

But fresh reporting by The New York Times unearthed documentary evidence and previously unreported instances of Mr. Milstein’s effort to skew information to the benefit of the Netanyahu government, which has continued throughout this year.

The Times interviewed 15 U.S. officials for this article, including many in Washington, all of whom worked with Mr. Milstein in some manner. The Times also talked to nine former diplomats who provided context on the role and responsibilities of senior embassy officials. All spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. The Times also obtained or reviewed dozens of documents, cables, memos and other internal communications.

The people who spoke to The Times were career government officials and political appointees, including strong supporters of the United States-Israel relationship. Most said they were speaking out of concern that Mr. Milstein’s actions are undermining standard diplomatic work, expressing worry that, in some cases, they contradict the president’s stated policies.

The concern extended to senior administration officials in Washington, including in the White House, who have expressed frustration to colleagues over some of Mr. Milstein’s actions, according to four officials, who have either witnessed or been briefed on the dissatisfaction.

It is not clear whether Mr. Milstein’s interventions have affected White House policy. But since Mr. Trump declared a year ago that he would not allow Israel to annex the West Bank, he has said little about the issue beyond briefly reaffirming in February that he opposed annexation, even as Israel was extending more control over the territory.

In response to questions sent to the embassy about Mr. Milstein’s actions, Mr. Huckabee did not address specific instances cited by The Times. He wrote in a statement: “The elements of the story The New York Times is trying to assemble are so lacking in fact that it ranks up with other Times farcical endeavors.” He added: “I personally and categorically refute the elements of your proposed ‘story.’ ”

Asked about The Times’s reporting on Mr. Milstein, the State Department provided the following statement: “The entire team at State remains focused on advancing President Trump’s America First agenda.”

The White House referred The Times to the State Department.

Mr. Milstein is the stepson of the right-wing radio host Mark Levin — a close ally of both Mr. Trump and Mr. Netanyahu. That relationship is well known in Washington and the embassy, and has been a factor in how he is treated, officials in both Jerusalem and Washington said.

As an adviser to Mr. Huckabee, Mr. Milstein is one of the most senior officials in the embassy, acting as a chief of staff of sorts to Mr. Huckabee. The ambassador has empowered him to oversee much of the mission’s portfolio, particularly the West Bank and Gaza.

Previous ambassadors to Israel have had political appointees as senior advisers who, like Mr. Milstein, tried to influence the reporting back to Washington. And Mr. Milstein’s responsibilities include reviewing and amending information sent to Washington.

People who interact with Mr. Milstein professionally, however, say he goes to unusual lengths to frame Israel in a positive light. He has blocked reporting from being sent, rewritten cables to deliver a different — sometimes opposite — message from the original, and delayed approving drafts until the topic was no longer relevant, these officials said.

In the summer of 2025, for instance, dozens of Palestinians seeking food were killed near the distribution sites run by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, backed by Israel and the United States. American diplomats in Israel drafted a cable, viewed by The Times, warning that the foundation’s distribution process was chaotic and deadly and risked more “mass casualty events.”

Mr. Milstein rewrote the cable to declare GHF’s operation a success while overlooking the mass casualties, according to people who saw the cable and were briefed on the editing process.

Troubled by glaring discrepancies between news coverage and the embassy’s official reports, White House and State Department officials seeking a clearer picture of events bypassed standard channels at least twice to communicate directly with embassy staff, according to two officials briefed on the outreach and an internal communication from late this summer seen by The Times.

Veteran American diplomats said that withholding or twisting the information sent to Washington should raise serious concerns.

“The embassy ought to tell Washington everything — the good, the bad and the ugly,” said Dan Kurtzer, who was the U.S. ambassador to Israel under President George W. Bush. “If they’re not doing so, they are damaging the policy-making process and possibly undermining the president’s policies.”

Mr. Milstein also questioned several colleagues on whether they were “pro-Israel” or “pro-Hamas,” according to four officials, who found the question inappropriate and said it made some people fearful of speaking freely.

A conservative and longtime Republican, Mr. Milstein served as an aide to Senator Ted Cruz of Texas from 2013 to 2018 before relocating to Israel to study at a Jerusalem yeshiva, a school for Jewish religious studies. In 2020, he landed a job as an assistant to David M. Friedman, Mr. Trump’s ambassador to Israel between 2017 to 2021.

During the Biden Administration, Mr. Milstein worked for Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, handling outreach to pro-Israel voters.

In April 2025, Mr. Milstein was back at the embassy in Jerusalem after Mr. Trump was elected to a second term.

In February, Nasrallah Abu Siyam, 19, was trying to stop settlers from stealing livestock when one of them shot him dead in his West Bank village.

He was the ninth American citizen of Palestinian or Turkish heritage killed in the West Bank by Israeli settlers or soldiers in four years. Weeks later, seeking an update on the investigations into the killings, 30 members of Congress led by Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland, sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanding answers from Israel.

In response, officers in the embassy compiled a report that was completed in March detailing the status of each investigation, according to multiple officials briefed on the process.

Its central findings suggested that, in most cases, investigations had made little progress, that some cases had been closed, and that no one had been charged in any of the killings, these officials said. Instead of forwarding the report, Mr. Milstein argued that the embassy should send a letter saying that Israel was properly handling the investigations, two officials briefed on the discussions said.

On May 4, Paul D. Guaglianone, a State Department official, sent a letter responding to Mr. Van Hollen, saying that the embassy, which had reduced staff because of the Iran war, was focused on security cooperation with Israel and protecting Americans against Iranian attacks. (The intense fighting had wound down nearly a month earlier, after a cease-fire was struck on April 8.)

The letter, provided to The Times by Mr. Van Hollen’s office, said the embassy was working with Israel to “ensure accountability for these deaths.”

The response did not reassure Mr. Van Hollen.

“If you don’t get accountability, you endanger more American citizens,” he said in a phone interview.

In February, the Netanyahu government passed a measure that made it easier for Israelis to buy land in the West Bank, a move widely condemned internationally as speeding the way to annexation.

Any formal Israeli annexation of the West Bank, which Israel captured in the 1967 Arab-Israeli war, would carry immense consequences. But in embassy discussions, Mr. Milstein portrayed the government’s announcement on land purchases as a domestic matter with little significance to the outside world, according to two officials.

An embassy report sent to Washington, reviewed by The Times, said the Israeli policy was meant “to address humanitarian needs” of Israeli settlers, without detailing those needs.

A similar intervention occurred in April, when top Israeli military commanders publicly warned that West Bank settler violence could set off a new Palestinian uprising. Embassy staffers tried to alert Washington to those warnings, but Mr. Milstein prevented the reports from being sent as drafted, according to three officials.

In a cable viewed by The Times on which he is listed as the first author, Mr. Milstein praised Mr. Netanyahu’s “unprecedented new initiatives to combat” rising violence in the West Bank. The report’s title read, “Government Cracks Down on Escalating West Bank Violence.”

David M. Halbfinger and Isabel Kershner contributed reporting from Jerusalem.
